assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect are a new state of matter in which band topology, spin-orbit coupling and protected edge or surface states can be computed from first principles and compared directly with transport and photoemission. This is the kind of discovery I look for: a clear physical idea, a quantitative theory, and experiments that confirm it. Its influence on condensed-matter physics, including topological semimetals, superconductors and materials design, is very large.
assessment.attribution: The decisive theory is the Kane-Mele proposal of the Z2 quantum spin Hall phase in graphene (to my recollection), followed by the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal for HgTe. Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells (2007). Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a coherent three-person configuration, but it leaves out other major contributors, notably Zhang (deceased), Bernevig, Moore and Balents, and Hasan, who is on the list but cannot also fit into three places.
assessment.maturity: Mature. More than fifteen years of independent confirmation across HgTe, Bi-Sb, Bi2Se3-class materials and ARPES, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer the theory-led trio over a prize that includes the 3D topological-insulator experiments (Hasan and others) is unresolved.
Real graphene has too small a spin-orbit gap to realise the original Kane-Mele phase, so the theory's priority rests on the concept rather than on that material.
I am working from memory on the exact credit history and have not verified it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene combines a quantitative continuum-model prediction of flat bands with experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity. It opened the field of moire quantum materials, which is the sort of surprise quantum mechanics keeps delivering. Theory and experiment connect closely and the continuum model is quantitatively useful.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald 2011 calculation predicted the magic angle. Jarillo-Herrero's group reported the correlated insulator and superconducting states in 2018, and Cao, Fatemi and others in that group did much of the work. A trio of Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero is defensible and the list supports it. Other theory and experimental groups (for example Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov) are not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent replication of the correlated phases exists, but the origin of the superconductivity is still debated and sample-to-sample variation is large. Recognition is somewhat early, though the field is very active.
uncertainties: The superconducting pairing mechanism is not settled, so the physical interpretation of part of the discovery remains open.
Sample-dependent behaviour and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility.
The decisive credit between theory prediction and experimental discovery is unresolved, and I am relying on memory of the sequence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is a foundational method for strongly correlated electrons. It gave the first controlled treatment of the Mott transition and underlies DFT+DMFT, the standard way of combining electronic-structure codes with correlation physics. As a practitioner of computational electronic structure I regard its impact on real materials, spectra and phase diagrams as substantial and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt (1989) introduced the infinite-dimension limit, and Georges and Kotliar (1992) mapped it onto a quantum impurity problem. Müller-Hartmann also contributed in 1989. Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt is the usual trio on the list, but Metzner is not credited here and I regard his contribution as essential. The credit is therefore incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Decades of use and cross-checks against cold-atom and spectroscopic data, with known limits (local self-energy approximation, cluster extensions needed).
uncertainties: The Nobel Committee has seldom honoured a theoretical method, and some members may see this as a technique rather than a discovery of nature.
The exclusion of Metzner and Müller-Hartmann is an unresolved attribution problem under a three-name limit.
Quantitative predictive power for real materials still varies with the implementation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism is a third magnetic class with compensated collinear order but spin-split bands, set by crystal symmetry. It is a real conceptual advance in magnetism, supported by symmetry-based and first-principles theory, and relevant to spintronics. The idea is clear and original, and experimental spectroscopy such as ARPES and X-ray dichroism connects well to calculated band structures.
assessment.attribution: Šmejkal, Sinova, Jungwirth and collaborators formulated and named the concept (2019 to 2022), building on earlier spin-group and related theory work by others (for example Hayami, Yanase, Yuan and Zunger). Šmejkal, Jungwirth and Sinova is a plausible trio from the supplied credit, though precedence among groups is contested.
assessment.maturity: Early. Several experimental confirmations (MnTe, CrSb and others) were reported from 2024 but the field is only a few years old, and device-level consequences remain to be shown. Recognition is probably premature for 2026.
uncertainties: Priority claims by other groups are not settled.
Independent experimental verification is recent and limited to a few materials.
Practical impact is expected rather than demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2008 discovery of superconductivity in LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx opened a second family of high-temperature superconductors with a different electronic structure from the cuprates, and led to quick advances in materials and in understanding of multiband, magnetically proximate superconductivity. Electronic-structure calculations were central to understanding the Fermi surfaces and magnetism.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group made the decisive discovery and I would credit him alone. Mazin contributed an early and influential theoretical interpretation (s-plus-minus pairing) but this was one of several near-simultaneous proposals, and I would not place theory on par with the discovery. The three-person space is not needed.
assessment.maturity: Mature in terms of confirmation of the materials and phenomenology; the pairing mechanism remains debated, as in the cuprates.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism is not established.
Maximum Tc is well below the cuprates, which weakens the case for a prize on practical grounds.
Whether Mazin should share credit is an open attribution question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance, first in amorphous alumina junctions and then with coherent tunnelling in MgO, drives magnetic read heads and MRAM. The coherent-tunnelling mechanism is understood in terms of first-principles band-structure symmetry filtering, which I find compelling. The impact is considerable and follows the 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported room-temperature TMR in 1995. The MgO coherent-tunnelling breakthrough came in 2004 from Yuasa and from Parkin (not on this list), with Butler and Mathon providing the theory (also not on this list). The three listed names cannot fully represent the decisive contributions, so the credit is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Mature and technologically proven, with decades of independent confirmation.
uncertainties: Whether this is seen as a sufficiently distinct discovery from the GMR prize already awarded.
Absence of Parkin and of the theorists from the supplied credits leaves attribution unresolved.
The case rests heavily on technology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmions are topologically protected spin textures observed in real and reciprocal space and described by quantitative micromagnetic and atomistic theory, in an area I follow closely. They are a clear example of emergent topological behaviour in magnets and have led to a large research programme on spintronics.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer's group observed the skyrmion lattice in MnSi by neutron scattering (2009), Tokura's group made real-space observations by Lorentz microscopy in 2010, and Wiesendanger showed individual atomic-scale skyrmions in 2011. The theoretical prediction came from Bogdanov and colleagues and from Rößler, Bogdanov and Pfleiderer, and Bogdanov is not on this list, which is a gap in attribution.
assessment.maturity: The existence of skyrmions is well confirmed, but the promised applications (racetrack memory and similar) have not materialised, so recognition is perhaps premature.
uncertainties: Missing theory credit (Bogdanov) leaves the attribution incomplete.
Applications remain unproven.
Whether the discovery is a sufficiently large step beyond established chiral magnetism.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetoelectric multiferroics combine electric and magnetic order, and first-principles theory (Spaldin) played a clear role in explaining why they are rare and in identifying mechanisms, with strong experimental work (Ramesh on BiFeO3 films, Tokura on TbMnO3) behind it. The scientific interest is considerable and the theory-experiment link is good.
assessment.attribution: Spaldin framed the problem and gave the first-principles understanding, Ramesh made thin-film BiFeO3 with strong coupling, and Tokura's group found the spin-driven ferroelectricity in TbMnO3 in 2003. Kimura is credited with that discovery and is not listed here. The trio is reasonable, though not unique.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature as a field, but the strong, room-temperature magnetoelectric devices that were hoped for have not arrived, and the main effects remain modest.
uncertainties: The Nobel-level, single decisive discovery is hard to identify.
Practical impact is below early expectations.
Attribution depends on a contested history that I cannot verify.
